Permutation and reload checks establish consistency, not semantic correctness: a wrong endpoint, stable ID permutation or incorrect scoring function can satisfy all three. Metamorphic-testing research therefore recommends diverse relations and complementary oracles ([survey](https://www.cs.hku.hk/data/techreps/document/TR-2017-04.pdf)). Applied to causal NextItNet, use an independently specified endpoint fixture: for `[0,0,a,b]`, the readout must select position 3, whereas `count_nonzero−1` selects position 1. Inject distinct, known timestep features to test selection exactly; separately compare the backbone with a small independently implemented causal-convolution reference using identical weights. Include singleton, short and full histories. These are proposed checks grounded in NextItNet’s causal formulation ([paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf)).

For mappings, verify `decode(encode(raw_id)) == raw_id` for every catalog item, uniqueness, reserved padding/OOV IDs, and agreement among histories, targets, candidates and embedding rows. Crucially, anchor selected raw-ID/index pairs to an independently recorded preprocessing manifest: mutually consistent encoder/decoder permutations pass round trips. Vocabulary APIs illustrate why reserved-token offsets require explicit checking ([TensorFlow documentation](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/StringLookup)).

For exported prediction, compare raw candidate logits against the actual training model in evaluation mode, then against an independently computed scoring head using verified endpoint features and candidate rows. Exercise every category, unequal batch/candidate dimensions and boundary IDs; compare values with declared tolerances, not only rankings ([PyTorch verification](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/onnx_verification.html)). Shared preprocessing, mapping, readout or scoring helpers create common-mode oracle failures. Validate oracle sensitivity with deliberate endpoint, ID-offset, transpose and omitted-bias mutations; agreement between implementations alone cannot establish correctness.
